articles.title: Decode a JWT in JavaScript without a library (and why decoding isn't verifying)
articles.excerpt: When an API call fails with a 401, one of the first things to check is the token. Is it expired? Does it have the right audience, scopes or user ID? A JWT carries all of that in plain sight. You just…
articles.body: When an API call fails with a 401, one of the first things to check is the token. Is it expired? Does it have the right audience, scopes or user ID? A JWT carries all of that in plain sight. You just have to decode it. You don't need a library for that. Here's how a JWT is put together, a small decoder you can paste into the console, and the one mistake that turns this into a security bug. What's inside a JWT A JWT is three parts separated by dots: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz header.payload.signature Header : JSON describing the token, like {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} . Payload : JSON with the claims, like sub , exp , iat , aud , plus whatever your app adds. Signature : proof that the header and payload weren't changed, created with a secret or private key.

articles.body: Every launch site I run has the same page shape. Product name in the <h1> , then one line the founder wrote about the product right under it. That line is the lede. It's the first thing a person reads, and it's also what my templates reuse for the meta description and og:description . This morning I wanted to know what actually survives that reuse. So I pulled 20 random product pages from the sitemaps of six of my sites (Aura++, EarlyHunt, IndieHunt, MakerHunt, SideHunt and Uno Directory), 120 pages in total, and compared the founder's line on the page with the meta description in the <head> . All 120 returned 200. Checks ran Nov 23 2026, around 10:20 to 10:30 AM IST, plain curl plus a small Python script.

articles.title: dd Said Done. The Disk Disagreed: Practical Dirty Page Writeback on Linux
articles.excerpt: A 1.5 GiB file copy finished in 2.6 seconds on a VM whose disk sustains roughly 370 MiB/s. That is not a disk that briefly got faster. dd measured how fast the kernel accepted bytes, not how fast they…
articles.body: A 1.5 GiB file copy finished in 2.6 seconds on a VM whose disk sustains roughly 370 MiB/s. That is not a disk that briefly got faster. dd measured how fast the kernel accepted bytes, not how fast they reached the platter. That gap is the page cache, and it is one of the most useful lies in Linux. It is also where "the database said committed" turns into "the last 30 seconds of writes are gone" after a power cut. This is a practical tour of dirty page writeback: what the six vm.dirty_* knobs mean, why the real limit is smaller than the percentage suggests, and how to measure the delay instead of guessing. All live numbers below come from a Debian 13 VM (kernel 6.12.117, ext4 on /dev/vda1 , 8,134,240 kB RAM, no swap).

articles.title: How barcode check digits work (EAN-13, UPC-A, ISBN) with a tiny JavaScript function
articles.excerpt: The last digit of a retail barcode isn't part of the product number. It's a check digit, calculated from all the other digits, so a scanner can catch a misread or a typo. If you generate barcodes, val…
articles.body: The last digit of a retail barcode isn't part of the product number. It's a check digit, calculated from all the other digits, so a scanner can catch a misread or a typo. If you generate barcodes, validate product codes in a form, or import a product catalog, you'll eventually need to calculate or verify one. The good news: EAN-13, UPC-A, EAN-8 and ISBN-13 all use the same algorithm, and it fits in a few lines. The rule Take every digit except the check digit. Starting from the rightmost of those digits and moving left, multiply them alternately by 3 and 1 . Add everything up. The check digit is whatever you need to add to reach the next multiple of 10.

One camp sells you raw material: a dozen independent filters, each with its own set of sliders, that you snap together into whatever signal logic you think fits the market you trade. The other camp sells you a finished product: a single indicator, pre-tuned by its author, that gives you a signal the moment you add it to the chart. Both camps have loyal users. Both camps also have a graveyard of customers who bought the wrong tool for how they actually trade.

articles.body: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering
